episodes.title: 何を教えているの？
episodes.scene: エナジャイザー初日の休み時間です。アキがコーヒーを飲んでいると、オーストラリアのミアさんと、韓国のミンジュンさんが声をかけてきます。
episodes.q: ミアさんのクラスは、何人でしょう。
episodes.a: 26人です。トゥエンティ・シックス、と言っていました。ミンジュンさんのクラスは、30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Hi! Mind if we join you?
dialogue.ja: こんにちは。いっしょにいいですか。

dialogue.en: Sure, go ahead.
dialogue.ja: どうぞ。

dialogue.en: Thanks! I'm Mia. I'm from Brisbane, in Australia.
dialogue.ja: ありがとう。ミアです。オーストラリアのブリスベンから来ました。

dialogue.en: And I'm Min-jun. I'm from Seoul.
dialogue.ja: ぼくはミンジュンです。ソウルから来ました。

dialogue.en: Nice to meet you. I'm Aki, from Fukuoka, Japan.
dialogue.ja: はじめまして。アキです。日本の福岡から来ました。

dialogue.en: Nice to meet you too, Aki. So, what do you teach?
dialogue.ja: こちらこそ。アキは、何を教えているんですか。

dialogue.en: I teach fourth grade. Almost every subject.
dialogue.ja: 4年生です。ほとんど全部の教科を教えています。

dialogue.en: Oh, nice! I've got Year Three this year. Twenty-six kids, and they've got a lot of energy.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。わたしは今年、3年生です。26人いて、みんなすごく元気です。

dialogue.en: I teach science at a middle school. I've got about thirty students in each class.
dialogue.ja: ぼくは中学校で理科を教えています。どのクラスも、30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Sorry, thirteen or thirty?
dialogue.ja: すみません、13ですか、30ですか。

dialogue.en: Thirty. Three, zero. It's a pretty big class.
dialogue.ja: 30です。さん、ゼロ。けっこう多いですよ。

dialogue.en: Thirty? Wow. Some days my twenty-six feel like a hundred.
dialogue.ja: 30人ですか。すごい。うちの26人も、日によっては100人いる気がします。

dialogue.en: Ha! Tell me about it.
dialogue.ja: はは、ほんとそれです。

dialogue.en: So, is this your first Energizer, Aki?
dialogue.ja: アキは、エナジャイザーは初めてですか。

dialogue.en: Yes, it's my first time. I'm a little nervous.
dialogue.ja: はい、初めてです。少し緊張しています。

dialogue.en: Me too. But everyone seems really friendly.
dialogue.ja: ぼくもです。でも、みんなすごく親切そうですね。

dialogue.en: Yeah, you're going to love it. Oh, the next session's about to start. Do you want to grab a coffee first?
dialogue.ja: ええ、きっと気に入りますよ。あ、次のセッションがもうすぐ始まります。先にコーヒーを取りに行きませんか。

dialogue.en: Sure. Let's go.
dialogue.ja: いいですね。行きましょう。

sounds.point: ミート・ユー が ミーチャ
sounds.explain: ミート・ユー が つながって、ミーチャ、と聞こえます。トゥー も弱くなって、タ。ナイスタミーチャ、です。

sounds.point: ア・ロット・オブ が アロッタ
sounds.clear: They've got a lot of energy.
sounds.explain: ア・ロット・オブ が ひとかたまりになって、アロッタ、と聞こえます。オブ は、ほとんど消えます。

sounds.point: ウォント・トゥー が ワナ
sounds.clear: Do you want to grab a coffee first?
sounds.explain: ウォント・トゥー が、ワナ、になります。前の ドゥー・ユー も省かれて、いきなり ワナ から始まっています。

joke.en: Thirty? Wow. Some days my twenty-six feel like a hundred.

humor.why: 本当は26人なのに、100人いるように感じると、わざと大きく言っています。聞き手は数を信じるのではなく、にぎやかさに共感して笑います。
humor.cue: 本当の数のすぐあとに、ハンドレッドのような大きすぎる数が出てきたら、大げさの冗談です。

aki.en: Some days my class feels like a hundred kids, too.
aki.ja: わたしのクラスも、100人いるように感じる日があります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Mia. I teach Year Three at a public primary school in Brisbane. I've got twenty-six kids this year, and honestly, they're a really fun group. They're eight and nine years old, so they've got heaps of energy, especially after lunch. Honestly, by two o'clock, I need a nap more than they do. We start every day with a quick check-in. Everyone says how they're feeling, just in one word. It only takes about five minutes, but it makes a big difference. We share a set of Chromebooks with the class next door, so we use them for reading and for writing stories. My favorite subject to teach is science, because the kids love anything messy. Last term we grew beans in the classroom, and they checked them every single morning.
talks.gist: ミアさんは、ブリスベンで3年生26人の担任です。毎朝、ひとことで気持ちを言う時間をとっています。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Min-jun, from Seoul. I teach science at a middle school, so my students are about thirteen to fifteen years old. I teach five classes, and each class has around thirty students. That's a lot of names to remember! I usually learn all hundred and fifty names by February. Then a new school year starts. In my lessons, I try to do at least one experiment every week. The students work in groups of four. They use tablets to take photos and videos of the experiment, and then they share their results on a slide. Some students are really quiet in front of the class, but they write great comments online. So I think technology helps them join in. My goal this year is to let students ask their own questions, not just answer mine.
talks.gist: ミンジュンさんは、ソウルの中学校で理科です。毎週、4人のグループで実験をしています。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Yu-ting. I'm from Taipei, in Taiwan. I teach English and computer science at an elementary school. I see a lot of different classes, from first grade to sixth grade, so every day is different. With the little ones, we sing songs and play games. With the older kids, we do small coding projects. Right now, my sixth graders are making a simple game about recycling. They work in pairs, and they help each other a lot. Sometimes the game doesn't work, and they get kind of frustrated. But when it finally works, they're so proud. That moment is my favorite part of the job. Next month, they're going to show their games to the fourth graders.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんは、台北の小学校で英語と情報です。6年生は、リサイクルのゲームを作っています。

talks.en: Hello! My name is Wei Ling, and I teach math at a primary school in Singapore. My class is Primary Four, so the kids are about ten. There are thirty-two students in my class. In math, I like to use real things. For example, when we learn about fractions, we cut paper pizzas, and sometimes real fruit. The kids remember it much better that way. We also do a lot of talking in math. I ask them, how did you get that answer? And they explain it to a partner. At first, they found it hard. Now they're getting used to it, and some of them explain things better than I do.
talks.gist: ウェイリンさんは、シンガポールで4年生の算数です。分数は、紙のピザを切って学びます。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo. I'm a high school teacher from Manila, in the Philippines. I teach ICT, so, computers and technology. My classes are pretty big, around forty students. So, managing the class can be a challenge, you know? We don't have a device for every student, so they share, usually two or three students to one computer. That's actually not so bad, because they talk and solve problems together. This year, my students are making short videos about their community. They interview people in their neighborhood, and they edit the videos in class. Some of them are really creative. To be honest, I learn a lot from them. It's hard work, but it's never boring.
talks.gist: カルロさんは、マニラの高校で情報です。40人のクラスで、地域の人にインタビューする動画を作っています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Priya, from Bengaluru, in India. I teach third grade at a private school. I have twenty-eight students, and they're about eight years old. I teach English and social studies. My students love stories, so I use stories for almost everything. When we learn about our city, they talk to their grandparents and bring the stories to class. It's lovely, because the families get involved too. We have a smart board in the classroom, and once a week we use tablets. I'm here because I want to learn simple ways to use Google tools, without making things complicated for the kids. Every Friday, we pick one story and make a short slide about it together.
talks.gist: プリヤさんは、インドのベンガルールで3年生の担任です。英語と社会を、お話を使って教えています。

episodes.title: 数字を聞き取る
episodes.scene: エナジャイザーのグループワークです。台湾のウェイさんと、フィリピンのカルロさんが同じ机に来て、アキの学校のことを聞いてきます。
episodes.q: ウェイさんの高校は、朝なんじに始まるでしょう。
episodes.a: 7時30分です。セブン・サーティ、と言っていました。生徒は900人くらいで、先生は30人くらいです。

dialogue.en: Hi, is this seat free? I'm Wei. I'm from Taichung, in Taiwan.
dialogue.ja: こんにちは。この席、あいていますか。ウェイです。台湾の台中から来ました。

dialogue.en: Sure, go ahead. I'm Aki, from Fukuoka.
dialogue.ja: どうぞ。アキです。福岡から来ました。

dialogue.en: Hi Aki, I'm Carlo. I teach at a high school in Manila.
dialogue.ja: こんにちは、アキ。カルロです。マニラの高校で教えています。

dialogue.en: So Aki, how many students are at your school?
dialogue.ja: アキの学校は、生徒がなんにんいるんですか。

dialogue.en: Hmm, I'm not sure exactly. What about yours?
dialogue.ja: うーん、正確にはわからないです。そちらはどうですか。

dialogue.en: We have about nine hundred students. It's a pretty big school.
dialogue.ja: うちは900人くらいです。けっこう大きい学校です。

dialogue.en: Nine hundred? Wow. Mine's only around six hundred.
dialogue.ja: 900人ですか。すごいですね。うちは600人くらいしかいません。

dialogue.en: And how many teachers do you have, Wei?
dialogue.ja: ウェイさんのところは、先生がなんにんいるんですか。

dialogue.en: Around thirty, I think.
dialogue.ja: 30人くらいだと思います。

dialogue.en: Sorry, did you say thirteen or thirty?
dialogue.ja: すみません、13と言いましたか。30ですか。

dialogue.en: Thirty, not thirteen. Three, zero.
dialogue.ja: 30です。13じゃなくて、さんとゼロです。

dialogue.en: What time does your school start, Aki?
dialogue.ja: アキの学校は、なんじに始まるんですか。

dialogue.en: A little after eight. What about yours, Wei?
dialogue.ja: 8時ちょっとすぎです。ウェイさんのところはどうですか。

dialogue.en: Ours starts a lot earlier. Seven thirty.
dialogue.ja: うちはずっと早いです。7時30分です。

dialogue.en: Wait, did you say seven thirty? That's early!
dialogue.ja: えっ、7時30分って言いましたか。早いですね。

dialogue.en: Yeah. My first class always looks a bit sleepy.
dialogue.ja: ええ。1時間目の生徒は、いつも少し眠そうです。

dialogue.en: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight, you know?
dialogue.ja: ぼくは6時には起きられるけど、8時までは頭が働かないんですよね。

dialogue.en: Same here. I need my coffee first.
dialogue.ja: わたしもです。まずコーヒーがないと、だめなんです。

sounds.point: サーティ と サーティーン、強いところ
sounds.explain: サーティーンは、うしろのティーンが強く、長めに聞こえます。サーティは、前のサーが強く、うしろのティは短く軽く聞こえます。

sounds.point: キャン は弱く、キャント は強く
sounds.natural: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight.
sounds.clear: I can get up at six, but I can't think before eight.
sounds.explain: できる、のキャンは弱く短くなって、クン、に近い音です。できない、のキャントは強く長めに読まれ、最後のトは消えることもあります。

sounds.point: ディッド・ユー が ディジャ
sounds.clear: Wait, did you say seven thirty?
sounds.explain: ディッド・ユー が つながって、ディジャ、と聞こえます。聞き返すときに、よく出てくる形です。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Wei, and I teach geography at a high school in Taichung, Taiwan. We have about nine hundred students and around thirty teachers. Our school starts early, at seven thirty, so a lot of students look sleepy in my first class. My students are fifteen to seventeen years old, and we study things like maps, climate, and local geography. My favorite part of the year is our field trips. Twice a year, we take students to the mountains or the coast, so they can see the places they read about in the textbook. The students love it too, and they always come back with lots of photos. This year, I'm trying to use more digital maps in class, not just paper ones. I came to this event to see how other teachers use maps and technology together.
talks.gist: ウェイさんは、台中の高校で地理を教えています。生徒は900人くらいで、学校は朝7時30分に始まります。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Carlo, from Manila, in the Philippines. My high school has around six hundred students, so it's not huge, but it's always busy. The building is right next to a main road, so it gets pretty noisy, especially in the morning. Classes start at eight, and most students come by jeepney, a kind of shared minibus, or on foot. We have one computer lab with about fifteen computers, and that's where I teach ICT. With forty students in a class, the room gets really crowded, you know? My favorite place at school is the covered court in the middle. We use it for assemblies, sports, and our school fair once a year. At this event, I want to find simple tools that still work when three students share one computer.
talks.gist: カルロさんの高校は、生徒が600人くらいで、8時に始まります。コンピューター室には、15台くらいのパソコンがあります。

talks.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana, from Auckland, in New Zealand. I teach at a primary school with about three hundred kids. There are twenty-four in my class this year, and they're seven and eight years old. I try to bring Maori culture into everything I teach, not just one lesson a week. We start each morning with a short karakia, and the kids really look forward to it. When we learn about nature, we talk about the Maori names for plants and animals, not just the English ones. I've got one Chromebook between two students, so they work in pairs a lot, and they help each other really well. My favourite thing to teach is storytelling, because the kids love making up their own stories about our local mountains and rivers. I'd love to see how teachers in other countries bring local culture into their lessons.
talks.gist: ハナさんは、オークランドの小学校で24人のクラスの担任です。マオリの文化を毎日の授業に入れていて、朝はカラキアという短いお祈りから始めます。

talks.en: Hello, I'm Arjun, from Pune, in India. I teach physics at a high school, so my students are about sixteen or seventeen years old. I have five classes, and each one has around thirty-five students. So that's about a hundred and seventy-five students every week! I like to start each topic with a simple question, something they can guess before we do the experiment. For example, before we study forces, I ask them why a rolling ball stops. We don't have a lab for every class, so three science teachers share one lab room. We have to plan it carefully every week. My students use their phones to record slow-motion videos of our experiments, and that works really well for physics. I came here to learn more ways to use simple technology, without expensive equipment.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんは、プーネの高校で物理を教えています。35人くらいのクラスが5つあり、実験室は理科の先生3人で分けて使っています。

talks.en: Hi everyone, I'm Chloe, and I teach English at a secondary school in Hong Kong. My students are in Form One, so they're twelve or thirteen, and I've got about thirty-two in each class. A lot of my students study English outside school too, so the levels in one class can be really different. I try to give them choices. Stronger students can read a harder book, and others can read something easier. Then they share their stories in small groups. We use Google Classroom for almost everything now: homework, feedback, even group projects. Once a month, we do a speaking project. Students record themselves telling a short story, instead of writing it. A lot of quiet students do much better when they can practise first and record it later. I'd like to find more ways to help students feel confident when they speak, not just when they write.
talks.gist: クロエさんは、香港の中学校で英語を教えています。1クラス32人くらいで、月に1回、短いお話を声で録音する活動をしています。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Liam, from Vancouver, in Canada. I teach grade three at an elementary school, so my students are about eight years old. I've got twenty-two kids this year, which is a pretty normal class size for us. School starts at eight forty-five, which is a bit later than a lot of places, I guess. Every morning, we do ten minutes of quiet reading before anything else, just to settle everyone down. I've got one Chromebook for every two students, and we use them mostly for reading and simple writing. My favorite subject to teach is math, especially when we use real things, like blocks or coins, instead of just worksheets. This year, my goal is to get students to explain their thinking out loud, not just write the answer. I'd really like to see how school days are different in other countries.
talks.gist: リアムさんは、バンクーバーの小学校で3年生22人の担任です。学校は8時45分からで、毎朝まず10分間、本を読みます。

episodes.title: 相づちとリアクション
episodes.scene: 休憩中に、オーストラリアのジャックさんと、ニュージーランドのハナさんが、アキのテーブルに来ます。うまくいった授業の話を聞きながら、アキは、あいづちで話を広げます。
episodes.q: ジャックさんの授業で、生徒は何を作ったでしょう。
episodes.a: スパゲッティで作った橋です。ブリッジズ・アウト・オブ・スパゲッティ、と言っていました。いちばんじょうぶな橋には、本を2キロ乗せることができました。

dialogue.en: Hey Aki, anyone sitting here?
dialogue.ja: やあ、アキ。ここ、だれか座っていますか。

dialogue.en: No, go ahead. Have a seat.
dialogue.ja: いいえ、どうぞ。座ってください。

dialogue.en: Kia ora, I'm Hana. We were just talking about our lessons this week.
dialogue.ja: キア・オラ、こんにちは。ハナです。ちょうど、今週の授業の話をしていたところなんです。

dialogue.en: Yeah, I had a really good one. My maths class built bridges out of spaghetti.
dialogue.ja: そうそう。ぼくは、すごくいい授業ができたんですよ。数学のクラスで、スパゲッティで橋を作ったんです。

dialogue.en: No way! Spaghetti?
dialogue.ja: えっ、まさか。スパゲッティで、ですか。

dialogue.en: Yep. Honestly, I sort of made it up the night before. Each group had to build one that could hold as much weight as possible.
dialogue.ja: ええ。正直、前の晩の思いつきなんですけどね。グループごとに、できるだけ重いものを乗せられる橋を作ってもらったんです。

dialogue.en: So how much did the best one hold?
dialogue.ja: それで、いちばんよかった橋は、どれくらい乗せられたんですか。

dialogue.en: Two kilos of books! I couldn't believe it.
dialogue.ja: 本を2キロも乗せたんです。信じられませんでしたよ。

dialogue.en: That's amazing. How did the kids react?
dialogue.ja: すごいですね。生徒たちは、どんな反応でしたか。

dialogue.en: They went wild. A couple of them even wanted to build another one at home.
dialogue.ja: もう大さわぎでしたよ。家でもう1つ作りたい、という子まで、なんにんかいました。

dialogue.en: Aw, that's so cool. I had a good one this week too.
dialogue.ja: わあ、いいですね。わたしも今週、いい授業ができたんです。

dialogue.en: Oh, really? What happened?
dialogue.ja: へえ、そうなんですか。どんな授業だったんですか。

dialogue.en: I told them a Maori legend from our area, and they acted it out in groups. I don't know why, but they really loved it.
dialogue.ja: 地元に伝わるマオリの伝説を話して、グループで劇にしてもらったんです。なぜだか分かりませんが、すごく気に入っていました。

dialogue.en: That's awesome.
dialogue.ja: それは、すばらしいですね。

dialogue.en: So, Aki, what about you? Any good lessons lately?
dialogue.ja: で、アキはどうですか。最近、いい授業はありましたか。

dialogue.en: Actually, yes. I made a short animation for math. The kids watched it again and again.
dialogue.ja: はい、じつはありました。算数の短いアニメーションを作ったんです。子どもたちが、なんども見返していました。

dialogue.en: Oh, I love that. Some kids need to see it, not just hear it.
dialogue.ja: それ、すてきですね。聞くだけじゃなくて、見ないと分からない子もいますからね。

dialogue.en: Nice one, Aki. Okay, we'd better get to the next session.
dialogue.ja: いいですね、アキ。さて、そろそろ次のセッションに行かないといけませんね。

sounds.point: ワット・アバウト・ユー が ワラバウチュー
sounds.explain: ワット の おわりの ト が、次の ア とつながって、ら行に近い音で聞こえます。アバウト・ユー も つながって、全体で ワラバウチュー に近い音です。

sounds.point: ソート・オブ が ソータ
sounds.natural: I sorta made it up the night before.
sounds.clear: I sort of made it up the night before.
sounds.explain: ソート・オブ が ひとかたまりになって、ソータ、と聞こえます。オブ は、ほとんど聞こえません。

sounds.point: アイ・ドント・ノウ が アイダノウ
sounds.natural: I dunno why, but they really loved it.
sounds.clear: I don't know why, but they really loved it.
sounds.explain: ドント の ト が消え、ドント・ノウ が まとまって、ダノウ に近い音になります。前の アイ も弱くなり、アイダノウ、と一息に聞こえます。

shower.topic_en: A lesson that went really well

talks.en: Hi, it's Mia again, from Brisbane. I want to tell you about a science lesson that went really well. Last term, each group planted bean seeds in a little pot, and the kids made a chart to check them every morning. After about a week, most of the beans were growing, but one group's pot had nothing at all. They were pretty upset about it. So we talked about it as a whole class, and someone noticed the soil in that pot was completely dry. They'd forgotten to water it! The group started watering it every day, and a few days later, a little green sprout finally came up. The whole class cheered. Honestly, that taught them heaps about patience, more than any worksheet could. For the rest of the term, they checked that chart first thing every morning, before I even asked.
talks.gist: ミアさんの理科の授業です。水やりを忘れて芽が出なかった班が、毎日水をやるようにすると芽が出て、クラスのみんなが喜びました。

talks.en: Hi, it's Yu-ting again, from Taipei. My sixth graders are still making their recycling game, but last week we had a test day, and it went really well. Each pair set up their unfinished game on a tablet, and the other students went around and tried every single one. It was kind of like a mini arcade in our classroom. The testers wrote down any problems on sticky notes and left them next to the tablet. A few games had bugs, but their classmates helped fix them on the spot. Some pairs got great ideas, like adding extra points for sorting the trash correctly. By the end, everyone had tried at least five games. Next month, they're going to show the finished games to the fourth graders, and now they really want them to be perfect.
talks.gist: ユーティンさんの6年生は、作っているとちゅうのリサイクルのゲームを、おたがいに試す日をもちました。見つかった不具合は、その場で友だちといっしょに直しました。

talks.en: Hey, I'm Arjun, from Pune, in India. I teach high school physics, and I want to tell you about a lesson on simple machines. We built pulley systems with string and a few cheap plastic pulleys, and the students had to lift a bag of books using as little force as possible. At first, most groups just used one pulley, and it was still pretty hard work. Then one group added a second pulley, and suddenly the bag felt about half as heavy. When they showed the class, everyone wanted to know how they did it. So we stopped and worked through the maths together, right there on the board. By the end, every group had rebuilt their system, and the room got really loud, in a good way.
talks.gist: アルジュンさんの物理の授業です。滑車を2つにした班が、本の袋を半分くらいの力で持ち上げ、そのしくみをみんなで考えました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Sophie, from Manchester, in the UK. I'm on the leadership team, so I don't have my own class, and my story's a bit different. This term, we started a reading buddy scheme. Our Year Tens read with the Year Sevens twice a week. Honestly, I wasn't sure it would work. But the first session went really well. The younger kids were so excited to have a big buddy, and the older ones took the job seriously. Some of them even brought bookmarks to give away. One boy who never liked reading much asked if he could keep the same buddy every week. And teachers across the school have noticed the Year Sevens are calmer afterwards, too.
talks.gist: ソフィーさんは学校のリーダー職です。上級生が下級生と週2回、本を読むしくみを始めたら、初回からとてもうまくいきました。

talks.en: Hi, it's Carlo again, from Manila. Remember those community interview videos my students are making? Last month, we had a screening day for the first few, and it went really well. We don't have a big screen, so we used a projector on the classroom wall and closed the curtains. Forty students, all watching each other's work, and honestly, they were so respectful, even when a video had mistakes. One group interviewed a jeepney driver, you know, the colorful jeeps we ride in Manila, and the whole class was cheering by the end. A few students got kind of emotional, actually, because some of the people they interviewed talked about hard times. After the videos, we just talked as a class for a while. It was one of my best days this year.
talks.gist: カルロさんの高校で、先月、地域のインタビュー動画の、最初の数本の上映会をしました。ジプニーの運転手の動画では、クラスのみんなが歓声をあげました。

talks.en: Hi, I'm Jiwoo, from Busan. I studied in the U.S., so I brought back this idea called a morning meeting, where the whole class sits in a circle before lessons start. At first, my students thought it was a little strange, sitting on the floor instead of at their desks. But last week, we had our best morning meeting yet. We were just sharing weekend stories, and one quiet student who almost never talks told a really funny story about her dog. The whole class was laughing, including me. After that, she seemed more comfortable speaking up in class discussions too. It's only ten minutes a day, but I think it's changed how the class feels as a group.
talks.gist: ジウさんは、アメリカで知った朝の会を続けています。ふだん話さない子が犬の話でみんなを笑わせ、その子は授業でも話しやすくなったようです。
